# Book pages 153–471 # Constituted Text Only; Critical Apparatus Removed ## Section 2. Vaṃśa | Chapter 1 (Mt. 4.33–55)
The wise Svāyambhuva Manu, having performed most difficult austerities, obtained as his wife Anantā by name, who was richly endowed with beauty. || 33 ||
Manu begot Priyavrata and Uttānapāda upon her;
and Dharmas’ daughter was the beautiful woman named Sūnṛtā.
From Uttānapāda, Mantharagāminī obtained sons:
Apasyati, Apasyantam, Kīrtimant, and Dhruva.
In ancient times, Prajāpati Uttānapāda begot Dhruva upon Sūṇṛtā;
having performed austerities for three thousand years.
Then, by the boon of Brahmā, he attained that divine and immovable station;
making Dhruva his very own leader, the Seven Sages remain stationed there. || 37 ||
The maiden of Manu named Dhanyā gave birth to Śiṣṭa from Dhruva;
and Succhāyā, the daughter of Agni, bore sons to that Śiṣṭa. || 38 ||
That Ripuñjaya begot Kṛpa, Vṛtta, Vṛka, and Vṛkatejas upon Cakṣuṣa, the daughter of Brahmā, by his wife Vīriṇī. || 39 ||
Cakṣuṣa begot Manu upon Vīraṇa’s daughter;
that Cakṣuṣa, indeed, begot [Manu] upon Naḍvalā, the king’s daughter.
He begot ten heroic and stainless sons:
Ūru, Pūru, Śatadyumna, Tapasvin, Satyavāk, and Kavi. (41)
Agniṣṭut, Atirātra, Sudyumna, and Aparājita, and Abhimanyu as the tenth, were born of Naḍvalā. || 42 ||
From her thighs, the radiant Āgneyī gave birth to six sons:
Aṅga, Sumanas, Khyāti, Kratu, Aṅgiras, and Gaya. || 43 ||
Pitṛkanyā Sunīthā gave birth to Vena from Aṅga. O Brahmins, they churned the unrighteous Vena; from his hand was born the one of great splendor named Pṛthu, who begot two sons. || 44 ||
Antardhāna, however, begot Mārīca upon Śikhaṇḍinī.
From Havirdhāna, Dhiṣaṇā, the daughter of Agni, gave birth to six sons:
Prācīnabarhis, Sāṅga, Yama, Śukra, Bala, and Śubha. || 45 ||
The venerable Prācīnabarhis was a great Prajāpati;
by him, many offspring were brought forth from the Havirdhāna. || 46 ||
The lord begot ten sons upon his wife Sāmudrī, who was of the same caste;
all were named Pracetas and were masters of the science of archery. || 47 ||
Protected by their ascetic power, the trees shone everywhere throughout the world;
yet, at the command of the gods, Agni, the son of the Sun, consumed them. || 48 ||
Somaka’s daughter became his wife, renowned by the name Mārīṣā;
from them she gave birth to one son, Dakṣa, who was preeminent. || 49 ||
Immediately after Dakṣa, she gave birth to trees and all kinds of medicinal herbs, as well as Soma’s daughter, the river Candravatī. || 50 ||
And of that Soma, Dakṣa had eighty crores [of progeny];
I shall describe their expansion, which is well-established in the world. || 51 ||
Some became bipeds, while others were men with many feet; some had faces like monkeys, some had ears like spikes, and others had ears that served as coverings. || 52 ||
Some had the faces of horses and bears, while others had the faces of lions; some had the faces of dogs and pigs, and others likewise had the faces of camels. || 53 ||
The righteous-souled Dakṣa produced all the Mlecchas in great numbers;
having first created them by means of his mind, he subsequently procreated women. || 54 ||
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, and twenty-seven, known as the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), to Soma;
from those two, the entire world consisting of gods, asuras, humans, and others, was produced. || 55 ||
**Section 2: The Genealogy | Chapter 2 | Part A.** (Aligned with L. 63.1–21; Mt. 5.1–32; P.1. I. 6.1–33a; P.2.V. 6.1–33; cf. Kū.
16.1–16) O Sūta, tell us in full detail and exactly as it happened the origin of the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas!
Sūta (Pulastya) said: The creation of the ancestors is said to have arisen from resolve, vision, and touch;
from Dakṣa Prācetasa onwards, creation originated through sexual union. || 2 ||
O twice-born ones, hear now exactly how Dakṣa, having been previously commanded by the Self-existent One to "create progeny," first brought them forth. || 3 ||
But when the world did not attain growth while he was creating the hosts of gods, sages, and serpents, he then [proceeded] by means of sexual union.
Dakṣa begot a thousand sons upon Asiknī;
seeing those illustrious ones, he desired to create various offspring.
Nārada spoke to the Haryaśvas, the sons of Dakṣa, who had assembled there: "Having ascertained the dimensions of the earth everywhere, both above and below. (6)
"Therefore, O best of sages, perform the creation in detail!
Having heard those words, they departed in all directions. || 7 ||
Even now they do not cease, like rivers from the ocean;
for when the Haryaśvas had perished, Dakṣa Prajāpati [created them] again.
The Lord produced a thousand sons from Vairiṇī alone;
those brahmins, known by the name Śabalas, were assembled for the purpose of creation. || 9 ||
The sage Nārada spoke again to those brothers who had followed him, just as before: "Having ascertained the dimensions of the earth everywhere, O brothers... (10)
"Having arrived, you shall indeed carry out creation in particular!
They then departed by that very same path, following the way of their brother. || 11 ||
From that time forward, the younger brother does not seek the path of his elder;
by seeking it, he incurs suffering, therefore one should avoid that. || 12 ||
Then, when those too had perished, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, begot sixty daughters upon Vairiṇī at that time. || 13 ||
He gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa, twenty-seven to Śoma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi. || 14 ||
Two were given to the son of Bhṛgu, two to the wise Kṛśāśva, and likewise two to Aṅgiras; their names [shall be told] in detail.
Listen to the expansion of the progeny of the divine mothers from the beginning:
Arundhatī, Vasu, Yāmī, Lambā, Bhānu, and Marutvatī. (16)
Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and the beautiful Viśvā are declared to be the lawful wives; learn now of their sons! || 17 ||
The Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā; Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas; the Marutvats were born of Marutvatī; and likewise, the Vasus were born of Vasu. || 18 ||
From Bhānu were born the Bhānus; from Muhūrtā, the Muhūrtakas;
from Lambā, those named Ghoṣas; and from Yāmī was born Nāgavīthī.
Arundhatī gave birth to Saṃkalpa, who was born from the surface of the earth; now learn of the creation of the Vasus from Saṃkalpa! || 20 ||
Those radiant gods who pervade all directions are designated as the Vasus; learn now of their creation. || 21 ||
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. || 22 ||
Āpa had four sons: Śānta, Vaitaṇḍa, Śāmbo, and Munibabhru; they were the ones authorized to protect the sacrifice. || 23 ||
Kāla was the son of Dhruva; Varcas was born from Soma;
and Draviṇa and Havyavāha are known as these two sons of Dharma. || 24 ||
Then Kalyāṇinī bore Prāṇa, Ramaṇa, and Śiśira; thereafter, Manoharā, the daughter of Hari, obtained sons from Dharā. || 25 ||
Śivā obtained a son, Manojava, whose course was likewise unknown;
furthermore, she obtained from Anala two sons who possessed qualities almost equal to those of fire.
The son of Agni, Kumāra, was born in a clump of reeds; Śākha, Viśākha, and Naigameya were his younger brothers.
The offspring of the Kṛttikās is known as Kārttikeya;
the son of Pratyūṣa was the sage named Devala, who was a muni. || 28 ||
Viśvakarman, the son of Prabhāsa, was a Prajāpati and a master craftsman; he was the creator of palaces, mansions, gardens, statues, ornaments, and the like.
He is remembered as the divine architect (Viśvakarman) in relation to lakes, groves, and wells;
[and his other names are] Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Sureśvara, Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita; || 31 ||
These are declared to be the eleven Rudras, the lords of the hosts.
Of these mind-born ones, who bear excellent tridents— || 32 ||
There are eighty-four crores of them, and their sons are considered to be innumerable—the lords of the hosts who provide protection in all directions.
These indeed are the sons and grandsons born from the womb of Surabhi. || 33 ||
**Chapter 2: The Genealogy** **Section B.** I shall proclaim the sons and grandsons born of Kaśyapa’s two wives:
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Ariṣṭā, and likewise Surasā. (1)
Surabhi, Vinatā, Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, Khasā, and likewise Muni—learn now of their sons! || 2 ||
Those gods who were named Tuṣitas during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu are remembered as the twelve Ādityas during the interval of Vaivasvata. || 3 ||
Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumat, and Viṣṇu as well. || 4 ||
These twelve Ādityas, possessing a thousand rays each, are remembered as having been born as excellent sons to Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, by Aditi. || 5 ||
The sons of the sage Kṛśāśva are remembered as the divine weapons;
O Brahmins, these are the hosts of gods throughout the various Manvantaras.
In every eon they are born and likewise dissolved again;
thus we have heard that Diti obtained two sons from Kaśyapa.
Hiraṇyakaśipu and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa;
and from Hiraṇyakaśipu, similarly, there was born a quartet of sons: || 8 ||
Prahlāda, Anuhlāda, Saṃhlāda, and Hlāda;
and the long-lived son of Prahlāda, Śibi, and Bāṣkala. || 9 ||
Virocana was the fourth, and he obtained Bali as his son.
O twice-born ones, Bali had a hundred sons, of whom Bāṇa was the eldest. || 10 ||
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as well as Sūrya, Candra, Audrāṃśutāpana, Nikumbhanābha, Gurvakṣa, Kukṣi, Bhīma, and Bibhīṣaṇa; || 11 ||
There were many such as these, led by Bāṇa, who excelled in virtue;
and there was Bāṇa, the thousand-armed, endowed with the entire collection of divine weapons. || 12 ||
Pleased by his asceticism, the wielder of the trident dwells in his city;
he attained the state of Mahākāla and equality with the wielder of the Pināka bow. || 13 ||
Hiraṇyākṣa had a son named Ulūka, as well as Śakuni, Bhūtasaṃtāpana, and likewise Mahānābha. || 14 ||
From these [ancestors] came seventy-seven crores of sons and grandsons, who were exceedingly strong, possessed of massive bodies, of various forms, and endowed with great splendor. || 15 ||
Danu obtained from Kaśyapa a hundred sons who were arrogant in their strength;
among them, the exceedingly powerful Vipracitti was the chief. || 16 ||
Dvimūrdhan and Śakuni, as well as Saṅkuśirodhara, Ayomukha, Śambara, Kapila, and Vāmana. || 17 ||
Mārīci, Meghavān, Irāgarbhaśiras, Vidrāvaṇa, Ketu, Ketuvīrya, and Śatahrada. || 18 ||
Indrajit and Saptajit, as well as Vajranābha;
the mighty-armed Ekacakra, Vajrākṣa, and likewise Tāraka. (19)
Asiloman, Puloman, Bindu, the great Asura Bāṇa, Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and others such as these were the sons of Danu. || 20 ||
Prabhā was the daughter of Svarbhānu, as were Śacī, the daughter of Puloman, Upadānavī, who was the wife of Maya, and likewise Mandodarī and Kuhū. || 21 ||
Śarmiṣṭhā, Sudarī, and Candrā were the daughters of Vṛṣaparvan;
Pulomā and Kālakā were indeed the two daughters of Vaiśvānara.
To that great being of many offspring, who was the protégé of Mārīca, there were formerly sixty thousand Dānavas born from those two. || 23 ||
In ancient times, Mārīca begot the Paulomas and Kālakeyas, who were indeed incapable of being slain by the immortals and resided in Hiraṇyapura. || 24 ||
Having obtained boons from the four-faced Brahmā, they were nevertheless slain by Vijaya.
Vipracitti begot the Saiṃhikeyas upon Siṃhikā. || 25 ||
O king of kings, those who were indeed the thirteen nephews of Hiraṇyakaśipu were Vyāsa, Śalya, Nala, and Vātāpi. (26)
Ilvala and Namuci, Śvasṛpa and Añjana, as well as Naraka, Kālanābha, and likewise Śarabhaṅga. (27)
And Kālavīrya was renowned as the progenitor of the Danu lineage; the Nivātakavacas are recorded as the sons of the Daitya Saṃhlāda. || 28 ||
They were unslayable by all the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
yet they were slain on the field of battle by Arjuna, relying upon his strength. || 29 ||
Tāmrā bore six daughters from the seed of Mārīca:
Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugrīvī, Gṛdhrikā, and Śuci. || 30 ||
Śukī gave birth to parrots and owls according to the law;
likewise, Śyenī gave birth to hawks, and Bhāsī gave birth to ospreys. || 31 ||
The pure Gṛdhrī gave birth to vultures, pigeons, doves, and various birds, as well as swans, cranes, kāraṇḍava ducks, and plavas. || 32 ||
She gave birth to goats, horses, sheep, camels, donkeys, and even to Śugrīvī.
This lineage of Tāmrā has been declared; now learn of that of Vinatā! (33)
Garuḍa is the best among those who fly, and Aruṇa is the foremost of winged creatures;
likewise, there is this maiden known as Saudāmanī, renowned in the sky. || 34 ||
Both Sāṃpāti and Jaṭāyu were the two sons of Aruṇa;
and Babhru, the son of Sāṃpāti, was also renowned as Śīghraga. || 35 ||
Jaṭāyu’s sons were the renowned Karṇikāra, Śatagāmin, Sārasa, Rajjuvāla, and Bheruṇḍa. || 36 ||
The progeny of those birds—sons and grandsons—became infinite.
In ancient times, there were a thousand serpents born of Śurasā. || 37 ||
Kadrū, being firm in her vows, obtained a thousand sons from the thousand-headed one;
among them, twenty-six were renowned as the foremost subduers of enemies. || 38 ||
Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Karkoṭa, Śaṅkha, Airāvata, Kambala;
Dhanañjaya, Mahānīla, Padma, Aśvatara, and Takṣaka. (39)
Elāpatra, Mahāpadma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Balāhaka;
Śaṅkhapāla, Mahāśaṅkha, Puṣpadaṃṣṭra, and Śubhānana. (40)
Sañkhuroma, Nahuṣa, Vāmana, Pāṇina, Kapila, Durmukha, and also Patañjali are thus remembered. || 41 ||
The lineage of sons and grandsons of all these became infinite, though most of them had previously been consumed in the palace of Janamejaya. || 42 ||
Krodhavaśā gave birth to the Rākṣasa host named Sunāman;
a million of those fanged beings met their destruction at the hands of Bhīmasena. || 43 ||
In like manner, Surabhi, who was firm in her vows, gave birth to the host of Rudras, as well as to cows, buffaloes, and excellent women, from Kaśyapa.
The sage gave birth to a multitude of sages, as well as a multitude of apsarases, and likewise many kinnaras and gandharvas who were invincible. || 45 ||
Irā gave birth to all grasses, trees, creepers, and shrubs;
Khasā, however, gave birth to crores of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas. || 46 ||
These descendants of Kaśyapa, by the hundreds and thousands—O King, this is recorded as the creation during the Svārociṣa Manvantara. || 47 ||
Then Diti, who knew the dharma and was beloved by the immortals, gave birth to forty-nine Maruts from Kaśyapa, all of whom were dear to the gods. || 48 ||
## Section 2. Genealogy | Chapter 2. C. (Mt. 7.1–65; P. I. 7.1–66; P.2 V. 7.1–66.
The Sages said: (Bhīṣma said: How were the sons of Diti born—the Maruts, who are beloved by the gods?
And why did they enter into unsurpassed friendship with the gods, who were their rivals? || 1 ||
Sūta (Pulastya) said:
Long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, when their sons and grandsons had been slain by the asuras, [the goddesses], afflicted with grief, went to the excellent world of Bhūrloka.
In the sacred field of Syamantapañcaka, at the great pilgrimage site of Puṣkara on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī— on that auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī—
she, devoted to the propitiation of her husband, performed severe austerities. || 3 ||
Diti, the mother of the Daityas, being of virtuous vows, performed severe penance such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other fasts, subsisting on fruit while in the form of a sage.
For more than a full hundred years she remained overwhelmed by old age and grief;
thereafter, having been purified by ascetic penance, she questioned Vasiṣṭha and the other sages.
"May you tell me, sirs, of a vow that destroys grief for one's son and bestows the fruit of good fortune both in this world and in the next. || 6 ||
The sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha, spoke of the Madanadvādaśī vow and the full-moon vow of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
by whose grace she became free from grief for her son. || 7 ||
The sages said: (Bhīṣma said:
"O Sūta, we wish to hear; O Brahmin, I wish to hear about the Madanadvādaśī vow and the full-moon vow of the month of Jyeṣṭha."
By whom Diti again obtained forty-nine sons. || 8 ||
Sūta (Pulastya) said:
Listen from me in detail to that very same excellent account which was previously told to Diti by Vasiṣṭha and the others. || 9 ||
In the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight,
on the twelfth day, one who is firm in his vow should place an unblemished jar filled with white rice.
Likewise, it should be provided with various fruits and accompanied by stalks of sugarcane;
covered with a pair of white cloths and anointed with white sandalwood paste. || 11 ||
One should place a copper vessel filled with various kinds of food and mixed with gold according to one's means, along with jaggery, upon it.
Above that, one should place as desired a [morsel] resting on a plantain leaf, combined with sugar.
And to his left is Rati. || 13 ||
A man should offer perfumes and incense to the two of them, and have songs and instrumental music performed; in their absence, he should narrate the story of Kāma and Keśava. || 14 ||
One should bathe the image of Hari with fragrant water under the name "Kāma," using white flowers, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds.
One should worship Madhusūdana. || 15 ||
Having worshipped the feet for the sake of desire, and the shanks for the sake of bestowing good fortune, one should worship the thighs again with the mantra "to Smara."
With "mamnathāya," he should indeed touch the hips. || 16 ||
"To Svacchodara" [he offers] the belly; "to Ananga" the chest of Hari;
"to Padmamukha" the face; and indeed "to Pañcaśara" the arms.
"Salutation to the Soul of All"—with these words, one should worship Keśava on the crown [of the head].
Then, at dawn, one should present that water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. || 18 ||
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion, while one eats oneself without salt;
with devotion one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and utter this mantra: || 19 ||
May the Blessed One Janārdana, who can assume any form at will and who is designated as the bliss within the hearts of all people, be pleased with this. || 20 ||
By this procedure, one should perform everything as prescribed every month;
fasting on the thirteenth day, one should worship the imperishable Viṣṇu. || 21 ||
Having consumed a single fruit on the twelfth day, he should sleep upon the ground;
then, in the thirteenth month, [he should give] a cow filled with ghee.
One should give a bed equipped with all necessary furnishings to Anaṅga,
and a golden Kāmadeva.
And a white, milk-yielding cow. || 23 ||
In this world, he who remembers Smara— who is Viṣṇu, the Great Lord whose essence is bliss— attains excellent sons and good fortune. (28)
"Seeking happiness, one should meditate upon the Lord, the progenitor of the body, in whatever form one desires.
Having heard this, Diti performed everything in its entirety.
Kaśyapa, due to the greatness of his vow, arrived with supreme joy. || 29 ||
He again made her harsh, though she was endowed with beauty and youth;
he sought to entice her with boons, but she chose a supreme boon: || 30 ||
I choose this high-souled one of immeasurable power, capable of slaying Śakra and the destroyer of all the immortals, as my son. || 31 ||
Kaśyapa spoke these words to the powerful slayer of Indra:
"I myself shall grant this very thing here; however, O auspicious lady, let this be done. || 32 ||
"O lady of virtuous vows, let Āpastamba perform today the *putrīyā* sacrifice;
thereafter, I shall conceive a fetus that will be the destroyer of Indra’s enemy. || 33 ||
Then Āpastamba performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice with abundant offerings, and he offered oblations in full detail, saying, "May you become the slayer of Indra. || 34 ||
The gods were bewildered, and the Daityas and Dānavas turned their faces away;
then Kaśyapa placed the embryo in Diti and spoke to her again: || 35 ||
Your face is like the moon; your breasts resemble bilva fruits; your lips have the appearance of coral; and your complexion is exceedingly beautiful. || 35 ||
O large-eyed one, having seen you, I have forgotten my own body;
thus, O fair-hipped one, a fetus has been sown by my hand within your person. (35b)
O fair-faced one, you must exert yourself for this very embryo for one full hundred years in this very grove of asceticism. || 36 ||
O woman of excellent complexion, a pregnant woman must never eat during the twilight hours;
she should never remain nor travel at the roots of trees. || 37 ||
Nor [should he touch] household utensils such as the pestle and mortar;
he should not plunge into water, and he should avoid empty houses. || 38 ||
He should not stand upon anthills, nor should he be troubled in mind;
he should not scratch the ground with his nails, nor with charcoal, nor with ashes. || 39 ||
One should not remain constantly prone to sleep, nor should one avoid physical exercise; furthermore, one should not sit upon husks, charcoal, ashes, bones, or potsherds. || 40 ||
She should avoid quarreling with people and likewise avoid stretching her limbs;
she should not remain with her hair disheveled, nor should she ever be impure. || 41 ||
She should never sleep with her head toward the north nor toward the west;
she should not be without clothing, nor agitated, nor should she be one whose feet are unwashed. || 42 ||
She should not utter inauspicious speech, nor should she indulge in laughter and the like;
intent upon auspiciousness, she should always perform worship for her gurus. || 43 ||
She should perform her bath with water produced from all medicinal herbs; having performed the protective rites, being well-adorned, and intent upon the worship of Vāstu. || 44 ||
Having performed the protection ritual, she was intent on service and devoted to worship through her speech. || 44 ||

She should remain with a serene countenance, devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband; being of a charitable disposition, she should observe the practice of eating only at night on the third lunar day of the full moon. || 45 ||
A woman who acts in such a manner will especially be censured; and as for the son she may have—
Endowed with the increase of longevity like that of stone. || 45 ||
She should never reproach her husband under any circumstances, saying,
"I am emaciated" or "I am weak."
And old age has come upon me. || 45 ||
My breasts have shifted from their place and my face is wrinkled with folds;
otherwise, there would have been a miscarriage.
He attains it without a doubt;
therefore, by means of this practice, exert yourself within this womb! || 46 ||
"May it be well with you; I shall depart," he said, and having been told "So be it" by her, he vanished right there while all living beings were looking on. || 47 ||
Then she proceeded according to the ritual prescribed by Kaśyapa.
Thereupon, Indra also became afraid and approached the side of Diti.
Having left the abode of the gods, he remained there, desiring to serve her. || 48 ||
Indra, seeking a vulnerability within Diti,
became outwardly composed, his face serene and his mind undisturbed. || 49 ||
Not knowing that it was his own duty, he performed that auspicious act;
then, at the end of a hundred years, less by three days, she [appeared]. (50)
With her mind filled with wonder and joy, she considered herself to have achieved her purpose;
without washing her feet, she lay down with her hair disheveled.
In one place, overcome by the weight of sleep, she lay with her head toward the west during the day;
then, finding that opportunity, the husband of Śacī entered within.
The lord of the thirty gods split that embryo into seven parts with his vajra;
from it were born seven young princes, radiant as the sun. || 53 ||
Those seven boys were crying, but they were restrained by the enemy of the Dānavas;
as they continued to cry, Hari [struck] each one of them with seven blows.
The slayer of Vṛtra indeed cut it again as it remained within the belly.
Having thus become forty-nine [parts], they wept bitterly. || 55 ||
Indra restrained them, saying: "Do not weep again and again.
Then the slayer of Vṛtra reflected: "What is this? || 56 ||
"By the greatness of what dharma have these been restored to life?
Having understood through the practice of meditation that it was the Madanadvādaśī vow," (57)
Surely this is the ripened fruit of their worship of Kṛṣṇa;
even when struck by the thunderbolt, they did not meet with destruction. || 58 ||
"Since even a single one has attained multiplicity, being sufficient even when residing within the belly, these gods must surely be inviolable; let them be so. || 59 ||
"Since you, while staying as embryos, wept when told 'Do not cry,' let them be known by the name Maruts and become partakers of the sacrifice. || 60 ||
Then, having propitiated the Lord of Gods, he said again to Diti: "Forgive me;
this evil deed was committed by me while relying upon the science of statecraft (arthaśāstra)."
Having made the host of Maruts equal to the gods, the lord of the immortals placed Diti along with her sons upon a celestial chariot and led them to heaven.
O twice-born ones, the Maruts were born from that [portion] as partakers of the sacrificial share;
they did not reach unity with the Asuras, and for that reason, they became the favorites of the gods. || 63 ||
## Section 2: The Genealogy | Chapter 3 (Mt. 8.1–12; P.1 I. 7.68–80; P.2 V.
7.68–80) The Sages said: (Bhīṣma said: "O Sūta, the primary creation has indeed been described by you in detail."
And tell us of the secondary creation and those who were their presiding lords! || 1 ||
Sūta (Pulastya) said:
When Pṛthu was consecrated as the sovereign over the entire earth,
he likewise made Soma the lord of the twice-born, of vows, and of austerities.
He was like the golden womb of the expanse of constellations, stars, birds, trees, shrubs, and climbing creepers;
likewise, he was Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, and Vaiśravaṇa, the sovereign of wealth and kings. || 3 ||
He made Viṣṇu the lord of the Ravis, Agni the lord of the Vasus and the sovereign of the worlds;
he made Dakṣa the lord of the Prajāpatis, and Śakra the supreme ruler of the Maruts. || 4 ||
Then [he saw] Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas; Yama, the lord of the Pitṛs;
and Śūlapāṇi, the king of the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Paśus, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, and Vetālas. || 5 ||
He made the Snowy Mountain the lord of mountains, the ocean the sovereign of rivers, and Citraratha the lord of Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras. || 6 ||
He appointed Vāsuki, the lord of serpents of fierce power, as the chief of snakes, and made Airāvaṇa, known by that name, the lord of the elephants of the quarters. || 7 ||
He made Suparṇa the lord of winged creatures, and Uccaiḥśravas the king of horses;
the lion the lord of beasts, the bull the lord of cattle, and the Plakṣa tree the lord of all forest trees. || 8 ||
Then the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) again consecrated these as the lords of all the quarters:
he first consecrated the guardian of the eastern quarter by the name Sudharmā, the banner against enemies. || 9 ||

Then the Lord, the master of all, who contains the universe within his womb, appointed the one named Śaṅkhapada as the sovereign over the south; and thereafter, Īśa made Ketumān the lord of the western direction. || 10 ||
Prajāpati created Hiraṇyaroman as the lord of the northern quarter and the son of Megha;
even today, the lords of the quarters protect the earth while burning their enemies. || 11 ||
By these four, the king named Pṛthu was first consecrated on earth;
and when the Manvantara was attained, they alone established this Vaivasvata [Manvantara] upon the earth. || 12 ||

When the interval known as Cākṣuṣa had passed and the one called Vaivasvata had begun once more, he became the Prajāpati of this world of moving and unmoving beings, bearing the lineage-mark of the solar dynasty. || 13 ||
## Section 2. Genealogy | Chapter 4 (Mt. 10.1–35; P.1 I. 8.1–35; P.2 V.
8.1–35a) The Sages said: (Bhīṣma said: "It is heard that in ancient times the earth was enjoyed by many kings."
The "earthen" (pārthiva) [beings] exist through connection with the earth; but by connection with what does the earth itself exist? || 1 ||
"For what purpose was the name 'earth' (bhūmi) created, and is it a technical term? [The questioner asked.
Sūta (Pulastya) said: "And this [name] 'Gauḥ' is well-known. He spoke:
In the lineage of Svāyambhuva, there was a Prajāpati named Aṅga;
he married the daughter of Mṛtyu, who was exceedingly ill-favored.
There was one named Sunīthā, and her son in former times was named Vena;
he was a lord of the earth who was devoted to unrighteousness, lustful, and weak-willed.

Even one who acts contrary to dharma in the world and who abducts the wives of others [is not to be condemned], for the sake of the accomplishment of righteous conduct and for the welfare of the universe, [this was ordained] by the great seers. || 5 ||
Although entreated, he did not give it, fearing for his own impurity;
therefore, tormented by the fear of a kingless state, they killed him with a curse.
The sinless Brāhmaṇas churned his body with force;
from that body being churned, the Mleccha tribes fell out.
In the mother's body, by her own portion, he possesses a luster like black collyrium;
and by a portion of the father's portion, he is righteous and a performer of dharma.
He was born from the right hand, equipped with a bow, an arrow, and a mace;
his body consisted of divine splendor, and he wore a jeweled armor and armlets.
It arose from the exertion of Pṛthu himself, and from that Pṛthu was born;
having performed very difficult austerities, he was consecrated by the brahmins.
By the boon of Viṣṇu, the Lord attained sovereignty over everything,
having observed that the surface of the earth was devoid of Vedic study and the *vaṣaṭ* call, and bereft of dharma.
Then the one of immeasurable prowess, out of anger, prepared to pierce her with an arrow;
thereupon, assuming the form of a cow, the Earth endeavored to flee. || 12 ||
Pṛthu, with his flaming bow, followed behind her;
then, standing at one side, he said, "What shall I do? || 13 ||
Pṛthu also spoke these words: "O lady of virtuous vows, grant quickly what is desired by the entire world, both the stationary and the moving. || 14 ||
"So be it," said the Earth; and that lord of men, Pṛthu, milked her, having placed Svāyambhuva Manu as the calf upon his own hand. || 15 ||
That became milk as food, by which living beings subsist.
Then the sages milked [the earth], and Soma was the calf at that time. || 16 ||
Bṛhaspati was the milker, the Veda was the vessel, and austerity was the milk;
then the earth was milked by the gods, and Mitra became the milker. || 17 ||
Indra became the calf; the milk was potent strength.
For the gods there was a golden vessel, and likewise for the ancestors, a silver one. || 18 ||
Antaka was the milker, Yama was the calf, and Svadhā was the milk;
for the Nāgas, Alābupātra was the vessel and Takṣaka was the calf. || 19 ||
The milk was poison; from that, Dhṛtarāṣṭra became the milker once again.
This [milk], which torments enemies, was also milked by the Asuras into an iron vessel.
In the vessel was *māyā*; Virocana, the son of Prahlāda, became the calf;
and Trimūrdhan was the milker there, by whom *māyā* was set in motion. || 21 ||
And in ancient times, O lord of the earth, the Yakṣas, desiring invisibility,
milked the earth using Vaiśravaṇa as the calf and an unbaked clay vessel.
The earth was milked by hosts of pretas and rākṣasas for fierce blood;
Rāvaṇa, who resembles silver, was the milker, while Sumālī was the calf. || 23 ||
Furthermore, that earth was milked again by the Gandharvas together with hosts of Apsaras;
having made Citraratha their calf, they likewise obtained fragrances upon lotus petals. || 24 ||
The milker [of the Vedas] was named Vararuci, who had not yet reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Having heard this, Manu spoke again to Janārdana:
"O Madhusūdana, tell me of the deeds of the former Manus!"
All the Manvantaras, the deeds of the Manus,
the measurement of time, and the rain— these he described in brief.
Listen with a single-minded and serene soul, O son of Mārtaṇḍa!
In ancient times, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, there were gods known as the Yāmas. || 3 ||
The seven sages who were formerly known as Marīci and the others—Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Vibhu, and Savana; || 4 ||
Jyotiṣmat, Dyutimat, Havya, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu—these ten were the progenitors of the lineage of this Svāyambhuva Manu. || 5 ||
Having performed these secondary creations at each dissolution, they departed for the supreme state.
This account of the Svāyambhuva Manvantara has been told; hereafter follows that of the Svārociṣa.
The four sons of Svārociṣa, who possessed divine luster, were Nabha, Nabhasya, Prasṛti, and Bhānu; they increased his fame. || 7 ||
Datta, Agni, Cyavana, Tumburu, Prāṇa, Kaśyapa, and Aurva, as well as Bṛhaspati—these seven are remembered as the Ṛṣis. || 8 ||
And the gods known as the Tuṣitas appeared during the Svārociṣa interval;
they were Hastīndra, Sukṛta, Mūrti, Āpa, Jyotis, Aya, and Smaya.
The seven sons of Vasiṣṭha are remembered as the Prajāpatis;
this second Manvantara has thus been described, and hereafter— || 10 ||
I shall now proclaim the auspicious Manvantara of Auttami, in which the Manu named Auttami begot ten sons. || 11 ||
Īṣa, Ūrja, Tanūja, Śuci, Śukra, as well as Madhu and Mādhava, and likewise Nabhasya and Nabhas; || 12 ||
Saha was the youngest among them; he was noble and increased their fame.
The Bhānus were the gods there, and the Ūrjas are remembered as the seven ṛṣis. || 13 ||
Kaukuruṇḍi and Kuruṇḍi, Dālbhya, Śaṅkha, Pravāhiṇa, Mita, and Saṃmita—these seven were the augmenters of Yoga. || 14 ||
The fourth Manvantara, renowned by the name Tāmasa,
belongs to Kavi, Pṛthu, Agni, Akapi, and Kapi.
In the same way, those seven named Janya and Dhāman were the sages, in whom the hosts of gods called Sādhyas are said to have resided during the Tāmasa interval. || 16 ||
Akalmaṣa, Dhanvin, Tapomūla, Tapodhana, Taporati, Tapasya, Tapodyuti, and Paraṃtapa. (17)
Partaking of austerity, devoted to the practice of yoga, and always engaged in righteous conduct—all these ten sons of Tāmasa increased their lineage. || 18 ||
Likewise, hear now of the interval of Raivata, the fifth Manu:
Devabāhu, Subāhu, Parjanya, Somapa, and Muni. (19)
Hiraṇyaroman, Saptāśva—these seven are remembered as the Ṛṣis; and the gods are remembered as having arisen from Rajas and being composed of Prakṛti. || 20 ||
He is independent, a seer of reality, free from distress, the consumer of oblations, a monkey; he is disciplined, devoid of longing, virtuous, free from delusion, and an illuminator. || 21 ||
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Rudras, the Maruts, the Vasus, the Aśvins, and the Ādityas—likewise, these are remembered as the seven classes of gods. || 29 ||
And her ten sons, headed by Ikṣvāku, are remembered on earth;
in all Manvantaras, the seven great ṛṣis, having established the order of dharma, proceed to the supreme station. || 30 ||
These ten sons of the Manu Sāvarṇi are proclaimed as those who will come to be. || 33 ||
Raucya and others are likewise proclaimed as future Manus;
the son of Prajāpati Ruci shall be known by the name Raucya. || 34 ||
Likewise, there will be one named Bhautya, the son of Bhūti;
after him, the son of Brahmā known as Merusāvarṇi is recorded as the Manu.
Ṛta, Rtudhāman, Viṣvaksena, and Manu—these are proclaimed as the past and future Manus. || 36 ||
O lord of men, this entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, having been produced within each of its own intervals, is pervaded by these for a thousand yugas of years.

When the dissolution of the eon has occurred, they are liberated along with Brahmā. These twice-born ones perish again and again at the end of a thousand yugas; thereafter, they shall indeed attain union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu, beginning with Brahmā. || 38 ||
## Section 4: The Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 1 (Aligned with Mt. 11.1–39; P.1. I. 8.36–75a; P.2. V. 8.35–74; cf. A. 273.1–4; Kū. 20.1–4a; L. 65.2–17a.
"O Sūta, knower of reality, you ought to recount in due order the entire Solar Dynasty (Ādityavaṃśa) and the Lunar Dynasty (Somavaṃśa) exactly as they are. (1)
Sūta (Pulastya) said:
Formerly, Vivasvat was born as a son to Kaśyapa from Aditi;
he likewise had three wives: the queen Saṃjñā, as well as Prabhā. || 2 ||
The queen Raivatī, daughter of Raivata, gave birth to a son, Revata;
Prabhā gave birth to Prabhāta, and likewise Saṃjñā, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, gave birth to Manu. || 3 ||
Yama and Yamunā were born as twins;
then, unable to endure the effulgent form of Vivasvat, [she cast it into the waters].
He produced from his own body a blameless woman, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, who was radiant with her own form and beauty, known by the name Chāyā. || 5 ||
Seeing her standing before him,
Saṃjñā addressed her:
"O Chāyā, O fair-faced one, resort to my husband as your own."
"Protect my children with maternal affection!
Having said, "So be it," that woman of virtuous vows went to the god for the sake of her desire.
The god also desired her with the respectful thought, "She is Saṃjñā," and he begot Śāvarṇi Manu, who was in the form of a Manu. || 8 ||
And because he was of the same lineage (savarṇa) as Vaivasvata Manu, he was called Sāvarṇi;
from him were born Śanī, Tapatī, and Viṣṭī in due order.
The Sun-gods produced this woman named Saṃjñā from their shadow;
at that time, Chāyā showed even greater affection for her own son, Manu. || 10 ||
Manu told him that story of Yama, who, then overcome by anger, raised his right foot and threatened him. || 11 ||
And Chāyā cursed Yama: "This one foot shall become wounded, infested with worms, and a discharge of pus and blood! (12)
Overwhelmed by the curse, Yama reported to his father:
"O Lord, I have been cursed without cause by my mother in her anger. (13)
"O Lord, out of childishness, I once raised my foot against a moving creature;
though I was being restrained by Manu, she nevertheless pronounced a curse upon me. (14)
"Generally, she is not our mother, since she is unequal [to us] in affection.
The god spoke again to Yama: "What shall I do, O high-minded one? (15)
Whose suffering would not arise from [the pursuit of] pleasure? Or rather, the continuity of karma is unavoidable even for one in existence (bhava); what then to say of other living beings? || 16 ||
Kṛkāvāku shall eat the worms in your place;
he will also remove this moisture and blood, my child. || 17 ||
Thus addressed, the highly illustrious Yama practiced intense austerity at Gokarṇa-tīrtha out of detachment,
subsisting on fruits, leaves, and air.
While propitiating Mahādeva for ten million times ten thousand years,
Mahādeva granted him a boon.
Then the wielder of the trident was satisfied.
He chose the status of a world-protector as well as the imperishable realm of the ancestors, along with the power to examine this world consisting of both dharma and adharma. || 20 ||
Thus he attained the status of a world-protector under the wielder of the trident;
whereas he who performs [this act] attains a most sinful and censured state.
In this world, he incurs the disease of leprosy, joined with suffering. || 32 ||
Therefore, one who desires merit, pleasure, or wealth should never have the feet of the wise God of gods placed upon various sacred sites or shrines. || 33 ||
Then that Blessed One, the lord of the immortals, having gone to the world of Bhūr,
being afflicted by desire, sought pleasure with her mouth alone, like the sun.
Endowed with a massive equine form and great splendor,
Saṃjñā, overwhelmed by fear, became agitated in her mind.
We have heard that when [the seed] was emitted from his nostrils, fearing it might be another's, the two Aśvins were subsequently born from that semen. || 36 ||
Because they were born from the tip of her nose due to her having given birth, the two were called the Dasras and Nāsatyas;
and after a long time, having realized this, she attained supreme satisfaction toward the God. || 37 ||
Filled with joy, she went to heaven in a celestial chariot together with her husband;
Sāvarṇi Manu, however, even today performs austerities on Mount Meru.
Through the power of his asceticism, Śani attained equality with the other planets;
Yamunā and Tapatī likewise became two rivers again, and Viṣṭi, who is of a terrible nature, remained established as Time itself. || 39 ||
## Section 4: The Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 2 To Vaivasvata Manu there were ten sons of great strength;
of them, Ilā was born first through a sacrifice for offspring (*putreṣṭi*). || 1 ||
Ikṣvāku, Kuśanābha, Ariṣṭa, and Dhṛṣṭa, as well as Nariṣyanta, Karūṣa, and Śaryāti—these were all of great strength. || 2 ||
Pṛṣadhra and Nābhāga—all of them were divine and human.
Having consecrated his eldest son, the righteous Ila, as king, Manu [departed]. || 3 ||
He went once more to the abode of Mahendra for the sake of ascetic penance;
then Brahmā, the bestower of boons, arrived there to grant him success.
"Choose a boon, O son of Manu; may it be well with you, according to your desire.
He then spoke to the Lord, the lotus-eyed one born from the lotus: || 32 ||
"O Lord, O Lotus-born One, by your grace, may all the kings on earth, joined with the Dharma, become my subjects and my masters. (33)
Having said "So be it," the Lord of Gods vanished right there;
then, having returned to Ayodhyā, he established himself as before. || 34 ||
Then once, King Ila, mounted upon his chariot,
set out across this earth for the purpose of accomplishing a world conquest. || 4 ||
Wandering through all the continents and subduing the kings,
the powerful one went to the grove of Śambhu, drawn by his horse.
There is a great forest of reeds (Śaravaṇa), filled with wish-fulfilling trees and creepers, where Śambhu, the Lord of Gods, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, delights. || 6 ||
Long ago, Umā made an agreement there in the Śaravaṇa forest:
"Whatever being, even one with a male name, shall come to our grove," || 7 ||
All that shall become womanhood within a circle of ten yojanas.
King Ilā, unaware of the duration of the transformation, went to the Śaravaṇa forest.
Even as he entered [the mare], the horse then attained womanhood;
his entire manhood was taken away.
The king was struck with wonder at her female form. || 9 ||
Then there appeared a woman with full, high, and firm breasts, with elevated hips and loins, and eyes as long as lotus petals. (10)
Her face was like the full moon; she was slender, with eyes radiant with playful grace;
her long arms were raised from their roots; and her hair was dark and curled.
With body hair growing upward, a beautiful face, and speaking with a soft, faltering voice;
she possessed a dark-complexioned, lustrous complexion and the gait of a swan or an elephant. || 12 ||
Endowed with eyebrows like a bow and possessing slender, copper-colored nail-sprouts, that beautiful woman wandered in that forest and reflected: || 13 ||
Who here is my father or my brother, who is my mother? To which husband have I been given, and how long shall I dwell in the realm of spirits? (14)
And as she was reflecting, that woman of excellent complexion, Ilā, was seen by the son of Soma, whose mind was captivated by her beauty, together with Aṅgaṇā. || 15 ||
Then Budha, afflicted by desire, made an effort to attain her;
he appeared with a distinguished form, carrying a staff, a water-pot, and a book.
Having taken possession of a bamboo staff, carrying a sacred grass ring and a small hoe, he assumed the form of a twice-born man; wearing a topknot and earrings, he recited the Veda. (17)
Accompanied by his young pupils who were carrying sacrificial fuel, flowers, kusha grass, and water, he called out for Ilā while searching for her in that forest. || 18 ||
Having hidden himself within a circle of trees on the outskirts of the forest, he suddenly spoke with agitation, as if with reproach: || 19 ||
Having abandoned the service of the sacred fire, where have you gone from my house? This is now the time for your diversion; it is currently passing by. || 20 ||
"Come, come, O lady of broad and beautiful hips; for what reason are you so agitated?
This is the evening hour here at the monastery. || 21 ||
"Having performed the smearing [of the floor], decorate my house with flowers!
She replied: "O ascetic, I have forgotten all of this. (22)
"Tell me, O sinless one, about yourself, your husband, and your lineage!
Budha said to that slender woman: "O lady of excellent complexion, you are Ilā. (23)
And I am known as Kāmuka, a wise man of great learning;
born into a family of radiant ones, my father was a lord among Brahmins. || 24 ||
Thus, at his word, she entered the palace of Budha, which was filled with jeweled pillars and fashioned through divine illusion. || 25 ||
Residing in his palace, Ilā considered herself to have achieved her life's purpose:
"Oh, what conduct! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what wealth! Oh, what a lineage! (26)
"Oh, what supreme beauty there is in me, in her, and in my husband!
And so Ilā took delight with him for a very long time in the forest, as if in a house filled with every enjoyment, just like the palace of Indra. || 27 ||
Then, searching for the king, his kinsmen, the descendants of Manu headed by Ikṣvāku, went to the vicinity of the Śaravaṇa forest. || 28 ||
Then they all beheld before them an unsurpassed mare, standing there, radiant with the rays of her jeweled saddle. || 29 ||
Upon recognizing the saddle, everyone was struck with amazement:
"This is the horse named Candraprabha belonging to that great-souled one! (30)
"For what reason did he assume the supreme form of a mare?
Then they questioned the domestic priest, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa: || 31 ||
"What was this wonderful thing that occurred? Tell me, O best among those who know yoga!
Vasiṣṭha, having seen everything with his eye of meditation, replied: || 32 ||
Long ago, in the Śaravaṇa forest, a compact was made by the beloved of Śambhu:
"Whatever man shall enter here, he shall attain womanhood. || 33 ||
This horse has likewise attained womanhood along with the king;
yet, just as that Ila became a man like the Lord of Wealth, so too shall he [the horse] become a man. || 34 ||
In that very manner, an effort must be made after having propitiated the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Thereupon, those men went to where the god Maheśvara was. || 35 ||
They praised Pārvatī and Parameśvara with various hymns.
They both said: "This convention is not to be transgressed; however, at present—" (36)
Whatever fruit might come from Ikṣvāku’s horse sacrifice, let that be ours;
having given it, that hero will undoubtedly become a Kimpuruṣa. || 37 ||
Having said, "So be it," those sons of Vaivasvata then departed;
and from the horse sacrifice of Ikṣvāku,
Elā became a Kimpuruṣa.
Ila was also called Sudyumna during his existence as a Kimpuruṣa;
furthermore, three sons were born to Sudyumna who were unconquered. || 43 ||
Then there were Utkala, Gaya, and likewise the powerful Dharitāśva.
From Utkala came the land named Utkalā, and from Gaya, the city of Gayā. || 44 ||
The eastern direction was recognized by the Kurus as belonging to Haritāśva;
he then consecrated his son Purūravas at Pratiṣṭhāna.
Subsisting on fruits, Ikṣvāku, the eldest heir, lived for a divine year in Elāvṛta to enjoy it, and then reached the Middle Country. || 46 ||
The son of Nariṣyanta was the mighty Śuka by name;
Nābhāga’s son was Ambarīṣa, while Dhṛṣṭa had three sons.
Dhṛṣṭaketu was his son, who was devoted to his own duty, bold in battle, and heroic; also Ānarta by name, and a daughter named Sukanyā, born of Śaryāti. || 48 ||
Ānarta had a son named Rocamāna, who was full of prowess;
there came to be a country called Ānarta and a city named Kuśasthalī. || 49 ||
From Rocamāna was born Revu, and from Revu came Raivata;
furthermore, Kakudmin was his name, and he was the eldest of a hundred sons. || 50 ||
That daughter of his, Revatī, became the renowned wife of Rāma;
and from Kārūṣa came the many Kārūṣas, who are celebrated throughout the earth. || 51 ||
Pṛṣadhra was born as a Śūdra due to the slaughter of a cow and the curse of his preceptor.
O best of sages, listen as I recount the lineage of Ikṣvāku!
The divine king named Vikukṣi attained the status of being the son of Ikṣvāku. || 52 ||
He was the eldest of a hundred sons, and there were fifteen of his own sons;
these were the sons of Ikṣvāku by name.
Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍaka. || 52 ||
The best among them were one hundred sons, and their sons were fifteen;
those most excellent of kings were born to the north of Meru. || 53 ||
Furthermore, another sixty-four [thousand] became his subjects;
and the kings situated to the south of Meru have thus been proclaimed. || 54 ||
The eldest was named Kakutstha; his son was Suyodhana. His son was named Pṛthu, and Viśvaka was the son of Pṛthu. || 55 ||
Ārdra was his son, and from him Yuvanāśva was born; Śrāvasta, of great splendor, was born, and Vatsaka was his son. || 56 ||
By him, O best of the twice-born, Śrāvastī was established in the Gauḍa country.
From Śrāvasta came Bṛhadaśva, and from him Kuvalāśva was born. || 57 ||
In ancient times, having slain the asura Dhundhu, he attained the name Dhundhumāra.
To him were born three sons: Dṛḍhāśva and Daṇḍa, and yet another. (58)
And the renowned Kapilāśva was the powerful son of Dhundhumāra;
Pramoda was the son of Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son. || 59 ||
Haryaśva’s son was Nikumbha, and from him was born Saṃhatāśva; both Akṛtāśva and Raṇāśva were the two sons of Saṃhatāśva. Yuvanāśva was the son of Raṇāśva, and from him Māndhātṛ was born.
From Māndhātṛ was born Purukutsa, and Dharmasetu was the king. || 61 ||
And there was the renowned and powerful Mucukunda, a friend of Śakra;
Purukutsa’s son was Dussaha, the lord of the Narmadā. || 62 ||
Saṃbhūti was his son, and from him Tridhanvan was born.
The son of Tridhanvan was born known as Trayyāruṇa. || 63 ||
His son was named Satyavrata; from him, Satyaratha is recorded. His son was Hariścandra, and from Hariścandra came Rohita. || 64 ||
From Rohita, Vṛka was born; from Vṛka, Bāhu was born.
Sagara was his son, a king most righteous. || 65 ||
Sagara also had two wives, Prabhā and Bhānumatī; by them, desiring sons, the submarine fire Aurva was propitiated in the past. || 66 ||
Aurva, being pleased with them, granted an excellent boon according to their desire:
one [requested] sixty thousand sons, while the other requested a single son. (67)
Prabhā chose the progenitor of the lineage, while Bhānumatī chose many sons; she chose one son, Asamañjasa. || 68 ||
Then Prabhā, the daughter of Yadu, gave birth to sixty thousand sons—those who, while digging the earth in search of the horse, were consumed by Viṣṇu. || 69 ||
Asamañjasa’s son was indeed the famous Aṃśumān;
his son was Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha. || 70 ||
By whom the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā was brought down after performing austerities;
he was the son of Bhagīratha, and the grandson of Bhagīratha.
He was indeed known by the name Śruta. || 71 ||
He was renowned as Nābhāga. || 71 ||
From Nābhāga was born Ambarīṣa; from him Sindhudvīpa arose.
His son was Ayutāyu, and from him Ṛtuparṇa was born. || 72 ||
His son was Kalmāṣapāda, and from him Sarvakarman is remembered. Anaraṇya was his son, and Nighna became his son. || 73 ||
Two sons were born to Nighna, Anamitra and Raghuttama. King Anamitra went to the forest for the sake of destroying his enemies.
From Raghu was born Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa likewise was born Aja;
Dīrghabāhu was born from Aja, and from him Prajāpāla arose. || 75 ||
From him was born Daśaratha, who had four sons;
all were of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, and Rāma was his eldest.
Likewise, Vālmīki—the best of the Bhārgavas—composed the life story of him who brought an end to Rāvaṇa and increased the lineage of the Raghus. || 77 ||
His two sons were Kuśa and Lava, who increased the Ikṣvāku lineage;
from Kuśa was born Atithi, and Niṣadha was his son.
Nala was born from Niṣadha; from him Nabhas was born;
from Nabhas Puṇḍarīka arose, and from him Kṣemadhanvan is recorded to have been born. || 79 ||
His son was the heroic and majestic Devānīka;
his son was Ahīnagu, and after him came Sahasrāśva. || 80 ||
From him came Candrāvaloka, and from him Tārāpīḍa;
his son was Candragiri, and from him Bhānucandra arose; from him Śrutāyu was born, who was struck down in the land of Bhārata. || 81 ||
In the lineage born of Kaśyapa, only two Nalas were renowned:
likewise, the son of Vīrasena and the king of Niṣadha. || 82 ||
These kings, who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees, born in the lineage of Vivasvat and originating from the dynasty of Ikṣvāku, have been proclaimed here primarily. || 83 ||
## Section 4: The Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 3 | Part A. (Mt. 23.1–47; P.1 I. 12.1–42; P.2 V. 12.1–51.
Soma is the lord of the ancestors (*pitṛs*);
how did he become an expert in the scriptures?
Who, then, were the kings born in that lineage who increased its renown? || 1 ||
Sūta (Pulastya said): Long ago, at the beginning of creation, Atri was commanded by Brahmā;
that lord then performed a supreme penance for the purpose of creation. || 2 ||
That Brahman which produces bliss, which destroys the afflictions of the world, and which transcends the senses, lies within the interior of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra. || 3 ||
O Brahmins, the performer of peace, with a peaceful mind, remains within that eye through his majesty and ascetic power.
It is the producer of supreme bliss.
Because the Lord of Umā is presided over by Umā together with her;
having seen him, [one is purified] by an eighth part.
From thirst, Soma became pure. || 5 ||
Then, from his two eyes, there flowed down that essence born of water,
illuminating the entire universe, including all moving and unmoving beings, with its moonlight-like radiance. || 6 ||
Desiring a son, the quarters there received him in the form of virgins;
having become an embryo, he remained within their wombs for three hundred years.
And the quarters, unable to bear the embryo, released it;
then the Four-faced One, having gathered that embryo together, [united it]. || 8 ||
The Lord Brahmā made that man young and equipped him with all weapons; then he placed him upon a chariot drawn by a thousand horses and consisting of the power of the Vedas.
Having brought the world there, that Grandfather led it into his own realm.
There, the Brahman-sages proclaimed: "May he be our lord! (10)
The collection of the Vedas was likewise praised by the ṛṣis, the gods, the gandharvas, and the apsarases, as well as by Brahmā and others with sāmans dedicated to the deities. || 11 ||
As he was offering praise, there arose within him an even greater manifestation of splendor;
from the expansion of his brilliance, a multitude of divine medicinal herbs appeared upon the earth. || 12 ||
Therefore, its radiance is always greater at night;
for that reason, Soma became the lord of medicinal herbs and is also called the lord of the twice-born. || 13 ||
And this orb of the moon, which is the essence of the light of the Vedas,
always wanes and waxes during the bright and dark fortnights respectively. || 14 ||
And Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, gave him twenty-seven daughters,
who were endowed with beauty and charm and possessed great splendor.
Then, for ten thousand times a thousand padmas, the Moon-god, solely intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu, performed austerities. || 16 ||
Then the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Supreme Self, Janārdana, being pleased, said to him: "Choose a boon. || 17 ||
Then Soma chose a boon: "I shall conquer the world of Śakra;
let the enjoyers [of the sacrifice] appear visibly in my own abode. (18)
In the Rājasūya sacrifice, let the fourfold hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā be present;
and let the god Hara, the wielder of the trident, be our protector and guardian. || 19 ||
Having been told "So be it" by Viṣṇu, he undertook the Rājasūya sacrifice;
Atri was the Hotṛ, Bhṛgu the Adhvaryu, and the four-faced Brahmā the Udgātṛ. || 20 ||
Hari himself became his officiating priest (upadraṣṭṛ), while Sanaka and the others are recorded as the assistant priests (sadasyas) in that Rājasūya ritual. || 21 ||
Likewise, the Vasus were the Adhvaryu priests, and the Viśvedevas were likewise [the Hotṛs];
thus the three worlds were offered by him as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests. || 22 ||
Then, when the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) was completed, nine goddesses, their limbs tormented by the arrows of love and longing to behold his form, attended upon him.
Lakṣmī abandoned Nārāyaṇa, and Sinīvālī abandoned Kardama; Dyuti abandoned Vibhāvasu, and Puṣṭi abandoned the imperishable Dhātṛ. || 24 ||
Prabhā left Prabhākara, Kuhū herself left Haviṣmān, Kīrti left her husband Jayanta, and Vasu left Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci. || 25 ||
Then Dhṛti, abandoning her husband Nandin, took refuge with Soma alone;
and Soma, in turn, desired them as if they were his own wives. || 26 ||
Even those initiated priests who have mastered the Vedas and completed their sacrificial rites would not be able to restrain him, nor could the gods together with Indra. || 26 ||
But even sages who had enjoyed all pleasures, wearing matted hair and deerskins, were agitated at the sight of a young woman and instantly fell into a state of intoxication. || 26 ||
Young women, whether approachable or unapproachable, when afflicted by passion, are like beasts; they cannot be restrained, just as rivers cannot be held back during the rains. || 26 ||
At that time, he attained the status of the sole lord of the seven worlds through his ascetic penance. || 28 ||
Once, he saw her in a garden, adorned with many flower ornaments;
though her limbs were exceedingly delicate, she was exhausted by the weight of her broad hips and breasts even while gathering flowers. || 29 ||

And that lord of stars, afflicted by love, seized Tārā—the wife of the preceptor of the gods, whose long and beautiful eyes were as enchanting as the arrows of the bodiless god—by her hair on a secluded spot of ground. || 30 ||
She too, afflicted by love, took her pleasure with him, as if her mind had been captivated by the beauty of his form;
then, after sporting for a long time, the Moon departed from there, taking Tārā with him to his own home. || 31 ||
Though devoted to Tārā, he found no satisfaction even in his own home amidst the arrival of pleasures;
consumed by the fire of separation from her, Bṛhaspati became single-mindedly intent on meditating upon her.

The Lord of Speech was unable to cast a curse upon him, nor could he harm him by any means whatsoever—not by mantras, weapons, fire, or poisons, nor even through various magical rites (*abhicāra*). || 33 ||
Then, tormented by the god of love, he begged the god Soma for his wife;
yet, though thus entreated, Soma would not give her up, being bound by the snare of pleasure with Bṛhaspati.

When the Moon would not give her up by any means, even though Maheśvara, the Four-faced One (Brahmā), the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the world-protectors [beseeched him], then Śiva became intent on wrath. || 35 ||

Vāmadeva, who was renowned upon the earth and whose lotus feet were worshipped by many Rudras—then that Giriśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow, accompanied by his disciples and bound by the fervent devotion of Bṛhaspati, [arrived]. || 36 ||

Taking up the Ājagava bow, the Enemy of Tripura, the Lord of Beings honored by the Siddhas, set out for battle with Soma; his face was formidable with the fire of his third eye, which blazed with exceptional intensity. || 37 ||

Gaṇeśaka and the others departed together; they departed together with the lords of the Gaṇas, accompanied by sixty-four times twenty attendants. Then Ugramūrti, joined by many hosts of Yakṣa-lords, followed those who were stationed upon their chariots—[he himself] being the sixty-second [in addition to the twenty].
Of the Vetālas, Yakṣas, Uragas, and Kiṃnaras, [the number is] one Padma and likewise one Arbuda. || 39 ||
Accompanied by thirty-two million chariots, Soma also went there with his wrath greatly increased;

joined by the armies of the Nakṣatras, Daityas, and Asuras, and possessing the augmented splendor of Śanaiścara and Aṅgāraka, the seven worlds—including the earth, forests, islands, and oceans—likewise felt fear. || 40 ||
Pinākin, having seized his blazing weapons and possessing a vast fire, went forth against Soma himself;
then there occurred that great battle between the two terrifying and formidable armies of Soma. (41)

Increasing and intent on the destruction of all beings without exception, appearing solely as a blazing fire with sharp weapons and missiles, the entire army of both sides met its end through their fierce and sharp arms; thus the blazing weapons fell, burning the realms of heaven, earth, and the depths of Pātāla. || 42 ||
Rudra, out of anger, released the Brahmashira weapon, and Soma also released the Somāstra of unfailing power. || 43 ||
At the falling of those two [missiles] upon the ocean, the earth, and the intermediate space, there was terror;
and beholding that battle of weapons increasing for the destruction of the worlds, even the Grandfather [Brahmā] [was moved]. (44)
Having somehow entered within, he restrained [the moon] together with the gods:
"O Soma, why do you, who cause the destruction of people, perform this unrighteous act? This must not be done! || 45 ||

Since you, O Soma, waged such an exceedingly terrifying war for the sake of abducting another's wife, you shall become a malefic planet among people. You shall become a malefic planet among people; though you are indeed naturally tranquil, alas, at the end of the dark fortnight, there will be no time even to take up a weapon.
"O Lord of Speech, surrender this wife; O Lord of Speech, you must surrender this wife!
For there is no one who does not fall when another's property is seized; there is no one who maintains their honor when another's possessions are taken. (46)
"So be it," said the moon-garlanded one; thus, having become pacified, he withdrew from the battle.
Then Bṛhaspati, taking Tārā, went joyfully to his own home along with Rudra. || 47 ||
## Section 4: Vaṃśānucarita | Chapter 3 | Part B (Mt. 24.1–71; Mh. I. 3156b–3182; P.1 I. 12.43–98a; P.2 V.
12.52–109) Then, at the end of the year, [he appeared] resembling the twelve suns, wearing divine seats and garments, and adorned with celestial ornaments. (1)
The prince, resembling the sun, emerged from the womb of Tārā;
he was a learned scholar, versed in all treatises on worldly affairs, and the founder of the science of elephants. || 2 ||
That which is known as the *Rājaputrīya*, the renowned medical treatise of the king, is so called because Budha is considered a "king's son" (*rājaputra*) due to being the son of King Soma. || 3 ||
As soon as he was born, that powerful one eclipsed all splendors;
then Brahmā and the other gods, together with the celestial sages, arrived there. || 4 ||
Then, at the birth-ceremony festival in the house of Bṛhaspati, all those gods asked Tārā: "By whom was this young boy begotten? || 5 ||
Then, being ashamed, she said nothing at all to them;
though questioned again and again, that beautiful woman remained bashful.
After a long time he said, "Of Soma," and then the Moon took the son;
he gave him the name Budha and bestowed upon him sovereignty on the surface of the earth. || 7 ||
Then, having performed the consecration, the Lord bestowed [the gifts];
thereafter, Brahmā, accompanied by the celestial rishis, granted the appeasement of the planets.
While all beings were looking on, he vanished right there.
And in the womb of Ilā, Budha begot a most righteous son. || 9 ||
He who, by his own splendor, performed more than a hundred horse-sacrifices—he was renowned as Purūravas, honored by all the worlds. || 10 ||
Having propitiated Janārdana on a delightful peak of the Himavat mountain.
Having propitiated the Grandfather (Brahmā), the king then attained sovereignty over the worlds as the lord of the seven continents. || 11 ||
By whom millions of Daityas, beginning with Keśin, were torn asunder;
he whose wife Urvaśī became, infatuated by his beauty. || 12 ||
The earth, consisting of seven islands along with its mountains, forests, and groves, was protected by him, who desired the welfare of all the world, through righteousness. || 13 ||
Fame herself became his fly-whisk bearer, and she personally served as his attendant;
then, by the grace of Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods granted him half of his own throne. || 14 ||
United with virtue, he protected dharma, artha, and kāma through dharma;
dharma, artha, and kāma, filled with curiosity, came to see him. || 15 ||
Desiring to know his conduct—how he might look upon them all equally—the king then offered them water for their hands and feet, along with other honors, out of devotion. || 16 ||

Having brought three divine seats adorned with gold ornaments and having seated [the guests] upon them, he then performed worship, though only slightly, yet with even greater devotion toward Dharma. || 17 ||
And those two, Kāma and Artha, went toward the king in great anger;
Artha pronounced this curse upon him: "Through greed, you shall meet your destruction! (18)
Kāma also said: "O Prince, you shall suffer madness on Mount Gandhamādana due to separation from Urvaśī and because of your reliance upon the young women. || 19 ||
Dharma also said: "O King of kings, you shall be long-lived and righteous; your lineage shall endure as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars. (20)
It will increase a hundredfold and shall not perish on earth;
for sixty years, there will be madness born of the passion for Urvaśī. || 20 ||
"Before long, even his wife, an Apsaras, will come under his control.
Having said this, they all vanished; the king then enjoyed his kingdom. || 21 ||
Day after day, Purūravas went to see the Lord of the Gods;
once, having mounted his chariot that travels through the southern sky, [he departed].
Then, together with Śakra, he saw Citralekhā and Urvaśī being carried through the sky by Keśin, the lord of the Dānavas. || 23 ||
Having conquered him in battle by discharging various weapons, the son of Budha, seeking glory, released the Vāyavya weapon. || 24 ||
In former times, even Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, was utterly defeated by him in battle; he then entered into friendship with him and gave Urvaśī to Indra. || 25 ||
From that time forth, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) entered into friendship with him;
[he bestowed upon him] excellence surpassing all the worlds, strength surpassing all the worlds, vigor, fame, and fortune— [all these] upon that very Purūravas.
The wielder of the thunderbolt, being well-pleased, said:
"Let it be sung by Bharata; let it be performed according to the rules.
For the sake of Purūravas's delight, they sang that great deed. (27)
He initiated what was called the Svayaṃvara of Lakṣmī by means of Bharata, and commanded Menakā, Urvaśī, and Rambhā, "Dance! || 28 ||
There, Urvaśī was present in the form of Lakṣmī within the *nauarta* dance;
seeing Purūravas, she danced, tormented by desire. (29)
Because all the dramatic gestures had been forgotten—those which were known in former times—Bharata, out of anger at their separation from that [tradition] on this earth, pronounced a curse. (30)
For fifty-five years she will exist as a creeper, and Purūravas shall experience the state of a Piśāca in that very place. || 31 ||
Then Urvashi went to him and made him her husband for a long time;
but at the end of the experience of the curse, Urvashi [was reunited] with the son of Budha.
He begot eight sons; learn their names:
Āyu, Dṛḍhāyu, Vaśyāyu, Dhanāyu, Dhṛtimān, and Vasu. (33)
Divijāta and Śatāyu were both possessed of divine strength and vigor;
Āyu’s sons were Nahuṣa and likewise Vṛddhaśarmā.
Raji, Dambha, and Vipāpman were five heroes who were great chariot-warriors (mahārathas).
To Raji was born a hundred sons, renowned as the Rājeyas. || 35 ||
Raji propitiated the stainless Nārāyaṇa;
Viṣṇu, gratified by his ascetic penance, granted a boon to the lord of the earth. || 36 ||
At that time, he was victorious over the gods, asuras, and humans;
then a war between the gods and asuras took place for three hundred years.
The battle between Prabhāda and Śakra was terrifying; neither of them was victorious.
Then, questioned by the gods and asuras, the four-faced god spoke: || 38 ||
"Which of these two shall be victorious? he asked. "Where Raji is," he replied. Then the king, seeking victory, said: "Be our ally for the sake of triumph! (39)
He said to the Daityas: "If I become your lord, then it is enough.
That was not accepted by the Asuras, but it was accepted by the Suras. || 40 ||
"Be our lord and destroy the strength of our enemies!
Then all those who were indestructible even by the wielder of the thunderbolt were destroyed. || 41 ||
The powerful Indra became his son, pleased by that deed;
having formerly given the kingdom to Indra, Raji departed for asceticism. || 42 ||
Then, by the sons of Raji, who were endowed with the power and virtues of asceticism, Indra’s sovereignty was forcibly seized, along with his sacrificial share and his kingdom. || 43 ||
Then Śakra, fallen from his kingdom and oppressed by the sons of Raji, spoke dejectedly to Vācaspati: "I am being tormented by the sons of Raji. || 44 ||
"O Bṛhaspati, I have been defeated; for me there is neither a share in the sacrifice nor a kingdom.
O Lord of Wisdom (Dhiṣaṇādhipa), exert yourself so that I may regain my kingdom! || 45 ||
Then Bṛhaspati made Śakra proud of his strength by means of the performance of rites for pacifying the planets and through nourishing rituals.
Then, having gone there, Bṛhaspati, the knower of the Vedas, mounted his own celestial chariot and deluded the sons of Raji for the sake of the sovereignty of the gods. || 47 ||

Having established himself in the religion of Jina, which is outside the Veda, that knower of the Veda, the lord of intellect, caused those who had fallen away from the three Vedas [to follow it]. || 48 ||
Having fully recognized those outside the Veda who were endowed with the doctrine of logic, Śakra struck them all with his thunderbolt, for they had been cast out from the Dharma. || 49 ||
I shall now proclaim the seven righteous sons of Nahuṣa:
Yati, Yayāti, Saṃyāti, Udbhava, and Para. (50)
Śaryāti and Meghajāti—these seven were the increasers of the lineage. Yati, even while still in his youth, became a yogi and a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa). || 51 ||
Yayāti always made his kingdom with righteousness as his sole refuge;
Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, became his wife. (52)
And Devayānī, the daughter of Bhārgava, who was firm in her vows;
these were the five heirs of Yayāti, whom I shall now name: || 53 ||
Devayānī gave birth to two sons, Yadu and Turvasu;
likewise, Śarmiṣṭhā gave birth to the sons Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru. || 54 ||
Yadu and Pūru became the increasers of their respective lineages. || 55 ||
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was a king of true prowess;
he protected the earth and performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites. || 55 ||
Always worshiping the ancestors and the gods with great devotion and self-restraint, the unconquered Yayāti then conquered all his subjects. || 55 ||
That eternal king, protecting his subjects according to dharma, reached a most terrible old age that destroys beauty, O Nahuṣa. || 55 ||
Overcome by old age, that king, the monarch, spoke these words to his sons—
Yadu, Pūru, Turvasu, Druhyu, and Anu.
"Moving through desires in my youth together with young women, I wish to enjoy myself; O daughter, please grant me your assistance! || 555 ||
To him, his eldest son Yadu, the descendant of Devayānī, said:
"What need have we for your assistance in our youth? (556)
Yayāti said to his sons: "Let my old age be taken up by you! Then, with your youth, I shall enjoy the objects of the senses. (557)
"O dear sons, because I have performed long sacrificial sessions and incurred the curse of the sage Uśanas, my desire for pleasure has been frustrated; therefore, I remain unsatisfied. || 558 ||
"Let one of you enjoy the kingdom with my body; as for me, being young and fresh in my prime, I shall attain my desires through this new form. || 559 ||
The Yadus and others did not accept old age from him;
we have heard that the wise royal seer cursed them accordingly. || 5510 ||
Then Puru, the youngest, whose prowess was true, said to him:
"O King, wander as a mendicant; may you be happy through my body, which is fresh with youth."
"I shall take your old age and remain in the kingdom by your command!
Thus addressed, that royal sage, relying on the power of his asceticism, [consented]. (5512)
Then he transferred his old age into his high-souled son;
by means of the Paurava’s youth, the king regained his own youth. || 5513 ||
Then, by means of Yayāti’s youth, Pūru ruled the kingdom;
thereafter, at the end of a thousand years, the unconquered Yayāti [returned his own age].
That tiger among kings, possessing prowess equal to a tiger, remained there;
and Yayāti also, having sported with his two wives for a long time, [departed].
Accompanied by Viśvācī, he took delight again in the Caitraratha forest;
yet that highly illustrious one did not then attain satiety with sensual pleasures.
Having understood this with his mind, O King, he then sang this verse:
"Desires are never quenched by the enjoyment of desires. (5517)
Like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more.
Even the earth filled with jewels, gold, cattle, and women— || 5518 ||
"All that is not enough for even one person"; realizing this, one should attain tranquility.
When one never commits evil toward any living being at any time— || 5519 ||
Through action, mind, and speech, one then attains Brahman;
when one does not fear, and when others do not fear one. || 5520 ||
"When one neither desires nor hates, then one attains Brahman.
Having thus perceived the worthlessness of sensual pleasures, O King, the highly wise monarch—
Having concentrated his mind through his intellect, the king received back his youth from his son;
and having bestowed his own youth upon Pūru, he consecrated him as king.
As if unsatiated by his desires, he said to his son Pūru:
"Through you I have an heir; you, my son, are the one who shall continue my lineage."
"This lineage shall attain renown in the world as the Paurava dynasty.
Then that tiger among kings, having consecrated Pūru upon the throne, [departed]. (5524)
Having performed great austerities on the peak of Bhṛgutuṅga, he practiced excellent penance;
after a long time, he eventually succumbed to the law of time. Having undertaken a fast unto death together with his wife, he attained heaven.
I shall proclaim the lineage of Puru;
listen, O best of sages,
wherein those Bhāratas were born.
O Bharatas, increase in prosperity! || 56 ||
I shall proclaim the lineage of Pūru,
in which you were born, O King;
from Yadu, however, the Yādavas were born.
Where those two, Balarāma and Keśava,
[reside] for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden and for the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas. || 56 ||
## Section 4: The Genealogy | Chapter 4 (Mt. 45.4–21; P.1 I. 13.73–94; P.2 V.
13.75b–95) The *syamantaka*, the unsurpassed jewel of Prasenajit, was proclaimed to be the king of all jewels upon the earth. (1)
Placing that jewel upon his heart, he entreated him many times;
yet Govinda did not obtain it, for though he was capable, he did not take it away. || 2 ||
Once, while Prahasta was out hunting adorned with that [ornament], he heard a sound made by some creature within a cave. || 3 ||
Then, having entered the cave, Prasena indeed beheld the bear;
the bear likewise saw Prasena, and the bear was also conquered by Prasena. || 4 ||
Having killed Prasena, the bear then took that jewel;
but he was not seen, for having been slain by him, he had entered the interior of the cave and gone deep within the mountain cleft. Then the bear entered Prasena’s body. || 5 ||
But having learned that Prasena had been killed, Govinda became suspicious;
[along with his brother Satrājit, the other Yādavas, and others:
"It is evident that Prasena was killed by Govinda for the sake of the jewel. (6)
Prasena, adorned with the jewel-gem, had gone into the forest;
seeing him killed by that [lion],
Govinda replied:
I shall slay this man of evil conduct, for he has become an enemy among the Vṛṣṇis. || 7 ||
Then, after a long time, having gone out again for hunting, Govinda arrived by chance at the vicinity of the cave. || 8 ||
Seeing that great noise, the powerful king of the bears let out a roar;
hearing that sound, Govinda entered with sword in hand.
He beheld that mighty Jāmbavān, the king of the bears. || 9 ||
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, his eyes bloodshot with rage, swiftly seized that bear Jāmbavān with extreme speed. || 10 ||
Then, having seen the Lord through his Vaiṣṇava deeds,
the Blessed One was indeed pleased.
He caused him to shine by means of a boon: || 11 ||
"O Lord, I desire death at your hand by a blow from your discus;
and may this auspicious daughter of mine obtain you as her husband! || 12 ||
"O Lord, this jewel which I obtained after killing Prasena—O Master, let it be taken by you; here lies this jewel. || 13 ||
Then that powerful, long-armed lord, having slain Jāmbavanta with his discus, completed his task and brought back the jewel along with the maiden. || 14 ||
He gave this [gem] to Satrājit in the assembly of all the Yādavas. || 15 ||
Tormented by that false accusation, this Janārdana [was distressed];
thereupon all those Yādavas then spoke to Vāsudeva: || 16 ||
Indeed, it was in our minds that Prasena had been killed by you;
furthermore, Kaikeya’s daughter is the auspicious wife of Satrājit, who has ten sons. || 17 ||
To them were born one hundred and one renowned sons of his, famous and of great heroism; Bhaṅgakāra was the eldest. || 18 ||
Then Vratavatī gave birth to three delicate, lotus-eyed daughters from that very same husband who had broken his vow. || 19 ||
## Section 4: The Genealogy (Vaṃśānucarita) | Chapter 4 From Anamitra, the youngest son of the joy of the Vṛṣṇis, Śini was born.
Satyaka was his son, and Sātyaki was his offspring. (1)
Satyavat was the powerful grandson of Śini; his son was the unassailable Yuyudhāna, and Dyumni was the son of that Yuyudhāna. || 2 ||
Dyumna’s son was Yugandhara; thus are the descendants of Śini proclaimed. This lineage of Anamitra, born of the Vṛṣṇi clan, has now been explained. || 3 ||
And from Anamitra was born the Vṛṣṇi hero Yudhājita;
his other two heroic sons were Vṛṣabha and Kṣatra. || 4 ||
Vṛṣabha took the daughter of the King of Kāśī as his wife;
from Jayantī, however, a splendid son named Jayanta was born. || 5 ||
From him was born Akrūra, who was a constant sacrificer, exceedingly steadfast, learned in the scriptures, and fond of guests;
from him Śuddhakṣa was born, a giver of many sacrificial fees.
Ratnā was the daughter of Śaibya; Akrūra obtained her and begot eleven sons of great strength. || 7 ||
Upalambha, Sadālambha, Utkala, Āryaśaiśava, Sadhīra, Sadāpakṣa, Śatrughna, and Vārimejaya—[these were his sons]. (8)
Dharmabhṛt, Dharmavarman, and likewise Dhṛṣṭamāna—all these were born as the Pratihotṛ priests for Ratnā. || 9 ||
From Akrūra, by Ugrasenā, two sons who increased the lineage were born:
Devavān and Upadeva, who resembled gods. || 10 ||
And from Aśvinī, there were sons:
Pṛthu and Vipṛthu, as well as Aśvatthāman, Subāhu, Supārśvaka, and Gaveṣaṇa. || 11 ||
